episodes.210158: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front moved across Central Alabama from late on March 11 into the early morning hours of March 12. After initially only producing a few areas of wind damage, the line quickly intensified east of I-65. Around 1 AM CDT, several trees were downed across Coosa and Tallapoosa counties. Scattered tree damage was also reported in Montgomery before activity quikcly ramped up after 2:30 AM CDT. Multiple areas of rotation within the line produced three EF-0 tornadoes across Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties, along with numerous instances of tree and structural damage from straight-line wind in these three counties along with Bullock and Lee. The line exited into Georgia by 4:30 AM CDT.

episodes.210171: A southern stream shortwave phased with a digging northern stream upper trough over the OH/TN valleys the night of 3/11 into the morning of 3/12 bringing a strongly forced system into the forecast area. The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.

episodes.210768: Showers and storms developed ahead of a cold front during the morning of March 11th, with subsequent rounds of scattered activity progressing across the area throughout the day. A few strong to severe storms downed trees in Perry and Morgan Counties during the early afternoon. More storms and moderate to heavy showers then overspread the area as an upper level disturbance steered the front through overnight. Between a half inch and one and a quarter inches of rain fell across southeast Ohio, with heavier precipitation prompting minor flooding of Duck Creek in Washington County and Sunday Creek in Athens County. Impacts primarily included flooding of a few roads, fields, and low-lying areas next to the creeks. Precipitation tapered off from west to east behind the front, coming to an end in southeast Ohio early in the morning of the 12th.

episodes.211822: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments. It's along those stronger segments where multiple marine locations were impacted by severe wind gusts.
episodes.211823: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.

episodes.212139: After a very cold winter, a significant amount of ice, with substantial depth, developed on main-stem rivers across eastern New York. Periodic multi-day stretches of late-season, above-normal temperatures subsequently led to considerable ice melt over a short amount of time. This ultimately led to flooding in Warren County in early to mid March after an ice jam broke loose on the Hudson River from the Route 28 Bridge at The Glen in Johnsburg. NWS Albany was made aware of the flooding and its requisite impacts from communication with both local news outlets and emergency managers in the area. According to these sources, water and large chunks of ice flowed rapidly downstream towards the towns of Thurman and Warrensburg. In Thurman, portions of River Road became inundated, specifically near The Glen Bridge, by both rapidly flowing water and large pieces of ice. This lead to the closure of the road for several days. In Warrensburg, portions of the Warren County Fish Hatchery also became inundated with some water and ice from a nearby branch of the Hudson River. Additionally, Cronin's Golf Course, which lies right along the Hudson River, became inundated with significant amounts of water. Areal drone images from a local news outlet showed what appears to be the entire golf course covered in water and ice. Due to the substantial nature of this ice jam, flooding impacted these areas for several days after the initial onset.

A strong EF-1 tornado touched down south of Hwy 570 near Moak Rd in Pike County, MS. This tornado rapidly strengthened and grew in size as it tracked to the east-northeast causing destruction of a wood frame farm outbuilding and increasingly significant treefall as it crossed Kodiak Ln and Magnolia Pisgah Rd. While there was a high proportion of treefall associated with this tornado in this area, a significant portion was due to uprooted trees from soft soils due to recent heavy rainfall. As such, maximum sustained winds were estimated near 110 mph despite the heavy deforestation. This level of heavy deforestation spanning approximately 375 yards wide at peak width continued across Hwy 570 to Dye Ln where tree damage rapidly became less significant. It's estimated that this tornado rapidly lifted as it crossed Magee Rd.

An EF-1 tornado with peak estimated winds near 105 mph and max width of 300 yards touched down near Johnston Chapel Rd. A broadly defined area of uprooted and damaged trees was identified via high resolution satellite imagery near the beginning of this path which continued east-southeast across Old Brookhaven Rd and Interstate 55. This damage was corroborated by a storm report with pictures of numerous uprooted trees near Chapel Dr. The tornado began to strengthen and increase in size with complex multi-vortex behaviors evident according to the damage path present after crossing I-55. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted along US Hwy 51, Rollingwood Drive, and Johnston Station Rd. Additional tree damage was surveyed near Lakeside Drive on Southwest Mississippi Community College campus. The tornado continued east destroying a cinderblock dugout at North Pike High School. More tree damage was also identified on Barrett Drive and Jaguar Trail. Scattered pockets of wind damage were evident via ground survey across Barnett Rd and L.D. White Rd, but the most cohesive damage points representative of a tornado damage path were evident to the southeast as the multi-vortex tornado continued to produce patches and swaths of tree damage on high resolution satellite imagery near Hwy 570 and and River Ridge Rd. The tornado damage path evidently became incoherent after crossing River Ridge Rd and it's estimated the tornado lifted prior to reaching Hwy 44.

The first of three EF1 tornadoes within the Pleasant Grove area|began near or just before the Jones/Wayne County border along|Cleve Blackledge Road producing minor tree damage. The tornado|remained solely between Cleve Blackledge Road and Pleasant Grove|Road. It reached its strongest point just prior to reaching|Pleasant Grove Road where it caused significant tree damage|evident on Sentinel 2 satellite imagery. A small building to the|south of Cleve Blackledge Road also sustained significant damage|visible on the satellite imagery but was likely associated with|intense RFD winds rounding the south side of the tornado as|debris was thrown towards the southeast.

This is the second of three EF1 tornadoes within the Pleasant|Grove area, with the final two tornadoes featuring a unique|interaction as they continued to the east. This northernmost|tornado began north of the Old Highway 84 Loop and west of Harry|Pippen Drive where some trees were uprooted in a pond lying|towards the northwest. The southern extent of the tornado was|along Old Highway 84 Loop where a tree was lying towards the|east. Thorough review of Sentinel 2 satellite imagery revealed a|coherent damage track that crossed Pleasant Grove Altair Road,|ultimately merging with another tornado track that came in from|the southwest on Daniel Roney Drive. When these tornado tracks|came together, significant tree damage was observed along Daniel|Roney Drive with numerous snaps and uproots in a roughly 250 yard|wide swath. This tornado then remained the dominant one that|continued northeast before occluding due north across some|chicken farms along Pleasant Grove Altair Road with major loss of|roof paneling. No additional damage was noted north of the road,|with the tornado likely lifting after impacting the chicken|farms.

This is the third of three EF1 tornadoes within the Pleasant|Grove area, with these final two tornadoes featuring a unique|interaction as they continued to the east. This southernmost|tornado began southwest of Old Highway 84 Loop causing minor|sporadic tree damage. The tornado intensified to EF1 intensity as|it began to cause more significant tree damage visible via|Sentinel 2 satellite imagery southwest of Daniel Roney Drive. The|tornado merged into the northern tornado path along Daniel Roney|Drive. Due to uncertainty on which tornado remained dominant|towards the northeast, this tornado track is estimated to have|ended just after crossing Daniel Roney Road as it turned|northward into the other tornado track. The peak width is also|estimated at approximately 50 yards based on the damage corridor|southwest of Daneil Roney Drive. After review of available high|resolution Planet satellite imagery, it was determined the|tornado began slightly earlier just off of Highway 84 where minor|tree damage was observed in a persistent, narrow path that|continued northeast into Old Highway 84 Loop.

There were several areas of concentrated tree fall, particularly at a home on Highway 239 where at least 20 large pine trees were uprooted surrounding the home. A majority of the trees fell towards the east-northeast with the motion of the storm. The home itself sustained no obvious damage, but one tree did fall on a car in the driveway. Further west down 239, a large portion of the metal roof on the Barbour County Farm Center was blown into the parking lot, and several trees were also uprooted at the Barbour County Jail and Ventress Correctional Facility property along 239. The tornado first touched down west of Bryant Hill Road and moved|through a large pecan orchard snapping and uprooting numerous|trees.  The tornado moved across Bryant Hill Road and very rapidly reached max intensity as it approached Sleepy Hollow Road.  JGX radar data also confirms the presence of very strong velocities in the area near Sleepy Hollow Road as well.  The|tornado struck a mobile home community on the west side of Sleepy Hollow Road destroying 4 mobile homes, overturning a home and damaging several others.  One of the residents of a home was thrown approximately 40 feet from one of the destroyed homes.  In another home, there were 2 injuries as a result of the home being|flipped over and destroyed.  The overturned mobile home remained intact, however the anchors which were concreted into the ground were pulled out of the ground and hanging from the frame.  Numerous trees nearby the community and across the street were snapped.  The combination of the damage to the mobile homes and the scope of the tree damage nearby are consistent with high end EF1 to low end EF2 and the basis of the low end EF2 rating for this storm.  The tornado continued east toward Hwy 49 snapping and uprooting trees.  Two large silos had their tops ripped off with bricks and debris strewn all around the area near the silos.  The tornado crossed Hwy 49 snapping and uprooting trees in a pecan orchard and flipping 3 sections of a center pivot.  As|the storm continued east, a weakening trend was noted both on radar and the corresponding damage on the ground with mostly sporadic tree damage across Vegetable Road, County Rd 123 and County road 116.  The tornado lifted north of Juice plant road just east of County Road 116.

A tornado spawned just west of Hwy 74 or Mercer University Drive near Windy Hill|Drive where several trees were snapped and uprooted.  The tornado continued east crossing Mercer University drive snapping trees and entering a neighborhood where numerous home sustained damage along McCleary Lane and Lochewolde Dr.  The most severe damage to homes included broken windows, garage doors being blown in, portions of the roof removed, and entire sections of shingles removed which is consistent with EF1 damage. The tornado continued east crossing Tucker road snapping and uprooting trees. One of the more interesting damage indicators was a large electrical transmission pole which was knocked over and bent across Tucker Road.  This would normally have yielded a higher rating, however, upon inspection, a very large tree had fallen into the pole and initiated its collapse.
